about.p: This book teaches more than 3,000 new words and expressions at advanced (C1–C2) level. At this level you need between 6,000 and 8,000 words to express yourself fully, and you also need to know their subtle *connotations*, their *register* (how formal they are) and how they combine into *collocations*, compounds and fixed phrases. Each unit has a **left-hand page** that presents the words in texts, conversations and tables, and a **right-hand page** of exercises.

The units are grouped by topic (work and study, people, leisure, travel, the environment, society, the media, health, technology), then by basic concepts, functional vocabulary, word formation, figurative language and language variation. Study them in any order.

about.-: **Today** gives you new words every day from the next unit and brings them back for review. **Units** has each left-hand page with its goals, checks and practice; pass with 80%.
Write your *Over to you* answers in the app: they are saved, and Claude can check them when it is available.

about.tip: Where learners often make mistakes, the units give advice on how to avoid them. Notice collocations and register when you read: which words go together, and whether a word is formal, neutral or informal.

L.p: The night before a test, many students *cram*: they try to learn a great deal very fast. Working through *past papers* (questions from earlier years' exams) is useful revision, even for a *genius* (someone of extraordinary intelligence). Some facts, like dates or formulas, can be *learnt by heart*, but *rote-learning* – memorising through repetition alone – rarely gives real understanding. A *mnemonic* is a memory trick, such as a rhyme or a word made from first letters.

L.e: In the month before her finals, Priya buried herself in her books; by the exam she knew every topic inside out.

L.p: Many writers begin with a *mind map*, a diagram that links ideas visually. Next comes a *first draft*, which is revised before you *write up* the final version. Copying someone else's work and presenting it as your own is *plagiarism*, so always *acknowledge* (give credit to) your sources. Finished work must be *submitted* before the *deadline*; it is then *assessed* (marked) and you receive comments.

L.h: C Aspects of higher academic study

L.e: Dr Okafor carries out research on coral reefs and publishes in academic journals. Her students use open educational resources and order rare books through inter-library loan. The course is demanding, and a few students drop out in the first year, but those who pass their finals graduate as well-qualified marine biologists.

L.x: Academics publish in *academic journals* (not *academic magazines*).

L.p: A central question in education is *equality of opportunity*: does every child have a fair chance? Supporters of *selective* schools, which choose pupils by ability, argue that they help bright children *excel*; supporters of *comprehensive* schools, which take everyone, say that selection *perpetuates* inequality and creates a *two-tier* system. Critics see *elitism* as *inherent in* any system that favours the *better-off*.

*League tables* (= lists of schools from best to worst, based on results) may *perpetuate* (= make continue) inequality and create a *two-tier system*. *Better-off* parents and *well-endowed* schools (= receiving a lot of money from gifts) push children to the top, which may *depress* (= reduce) opportunity for the *less well-off*. A *scholarship* is given for academic merit; a *bursary* is given according to need. Student loans help *undergraduates* pay *tuition fees* in *tertiary* (= university or college) education.

L.tip: Compounds with *well* and *badly* can form comparatives and superlatives: *well-off* → *better-off*; *well-paid* → *best-paid*; *badly-behaved* → *worst-behaved*.

L.e: Politicians often promise a return to the three Rs – reading, writing and arithmetic – arguing that literacy and numeracy matter more than anything else. Teachers, meanwhile, struggle to get to grips with constant curriculum reform. The new guidelines say that every school must have a clear policy on bullying and support for pupils with special needs, including one-to-one help where necessary. Adult colleges promote lifelong education and welcome mature students.

L.e: Are you passionate about food and ready for a challenging role? Our busy, fast-paced kitchen has two openings for trainee chefs. You will report to the head chef and learn every part of the business. This post offers real career prospects for people with leadership qualities. We pay a competitive salary, and our benefits package includes subsidised gym membership. Please state your salary expectations when you apply.

L.p: *Challenging* = difficult in an interesting and rewarding way; *fast-paced* = with lots happening quickly; *opening* = a job vacancy; *report to* = have someone as your direct manager; *post* = position or job; *career prospects* = chances of moving up in the future; *competitive salary* = pay that matches or beats other employers; *benefits package* = extras such as health insurance or a pension; *subsidised* = cheaper because the employer pays part.
To make your application *stand out* from hundreds of others, send a short *cover letter* that *highlights* the experience most *relevant to* the job, rather than repeating your whole CV.

L.e: Dear Sir or Madam, I would like to apply for the post of trainee chef, and I attach my CV. Over the past two years I have gained hands-on experience in a busy café, which has taught me to work fast and stay calm. I enjoy working in a customer-facing role and see myself as a team player. In the long term, I hope to gain managerial experience in the field of hospitality. Yours faithfully, Tom Reid

L.p: When companies are *recruiting* (= hiring new staff), they use *criteria* (= requirements for making a decision) to find suitable candidates. If you are *shortlisted* (= selected from a larger group), *do your homework* on the company and ask a friend to do a *trial run* (= a practice) to *boost* (= increase) your confidence.

L.e: Before the interview, do your homework on the company, and do a trial run of the journey the day before. On the day, the panel will probably include your future line manager. Sit up straight, make eye contact and speak up so everyone can hear you. A firm handshake and positive body language help create a strong first impression.

Could you talk us through your last project? – Certainly. I joined the company as a trainee and was soon given more responsibility. – How do you deal with working under pressure? – I make a list and focus on the most urgent tasks. – What's your notice period? – One month. – Do you have any questions for us? – Yes: is there an in-house programme for professional development?

L.p: *Talk someone through* = explain in detail; *in-house* = within the company; *new recruits* = people who have just joined; *notice period* = the time you must keep working after you say you are leaving.

L.e: Dear Mr Lee, Following your interview, we are pleased to offer you the post of Junior Designer. The attached document outlines your duties, salary and paid leave. Your skills make you an ideal fit for our team. Please return the signed paperwork by 30 June.

L.p: *Job satisfaction* = the sense of achievement and enjoyment your work gives you; *run-of-the-mill* = average, not special; *financial reward* = the money you earn for your work; *staff morale* = how positive and confident employees feel; *teamwork* = people cooperating to reach a shared goal; *job stability* = security, with little risk of losing your job; *fast-moving* = changing quickly; *work–life balance* = a healthy split between your job and private life; *dynamic* = full of energy and new ideas; *demotivated* = having lost interest and enthusiasm.

L.e: After the pay freeze, staff morale at the factory hit rock bottom. Many workers feel demotivated and are looking for jobs with more job stability. Jake is seeking a career in a more dynamic, fast-moving industry.

L.tip: Group words that mean almost the same: *dynamic* goes with *fast-moving*, and *seek a career in* with *hope to work in*. In business English, *be looking to* + verb means 'be planning to': We're looking to expand next year.

units.sub: cold calling, loss leader, hammer out a deal

L.p: Ana's first job was in *telesales*, selling insurance over the phone. *Cold calling* – ringing strangers who hadn't asked to be contacted – was hard, and many people hung up as soon as they recognised *the hard sell* (aggressive selling). But she *persevered*, learned to listen, and became very good at persuading customers to *part with their money*. Later she opened a small online shop selling *merchandise* for music fans, and she *hasn't looked back* since.

*Purchasing power* is how much people can afford to buy. Careful buyers *shop around*, comparing prices in different shops. A shop *stocks* the goods it keeps for sale. When you *trade up*, you replace something with a more expensive version. Customers with *brand loyalty* keep buying the same make. Supermarkets sell some items as *loss leaders*, below cost, to attract shoppers. A *niche market* is a small, specialised group of buyers. Things that *go under the hammer* are sold at auction to the highest *bidder*.

Tina's software business turned out to be *lucrative* (= producing a lot of money), but she got irritated by the *red tape* (= bureaucracy) of *administration*. When a larger company made a *proposition* (= a formal offer) about a *takeover*, the two sides *reached a compromise* and *hammered out a deal*. Her company was *swallowed up*, but she used the money from the sale of its *capital assets* to *invest in* a *start-up*: a holiday *letting agency*.

L.tip: A *takeover* happens when one firm gains control of another, sometimes against its will; a *merger* is when two firms agree to combine into a single company.

L.h: A Size, weight and general appearance

L.p: *Slender* = thin in an attractive way; *scrawny* = unattractively thin and bony; *lanky* = very tall and thin, moving awkwardly; *gangling* or *gangly* = tall with long thin arms and legs, often of boys; *obese* = very fat in an unhealthy way; *stout* = with a large solid body; *stocky* = short with broad shoulders and chest.

L.h: B Aspects of appearance and complexion

L.e: After six months at the gym, my cousin has bulked up; he used to be lean and wiry like his father. My aunt is always immaculate – never a hair out of place – whereas her son usually looks unkempt. After three sleepless nights, the young doctor looked haggard. The fisherman had a swarthy, weather-beaten face; his wife's skin was pale and sallow.

L.p: *Bulk up* = gain muscle; *lean* = thin and healthy; *wiry* = thin but strong; *unkempt* = untidy ('kempt' does not exist); *immaculate* = in perfect condition; *swarthy* = dark-skinned; *sallow* = yellowish; *haggard* = looking ill and tired.

L.e: The little boy grinned when he saw the cake. When she didn't get the window seat, my daughter pouted for an hour. He grimaced as he swallowed the medicine. The head teacher scowled at the latecomers. A man at the bar was leering at the women, so they moved away.

When I asked where the keys were, he just shrugged his shoulders. During the argument she folded her arms and refused to speak. His left eye twitches when he's tired. He clenched his fists in anger. While she waited for her results, she drummed her fingers on the desk.

L.e: After a week of camping, I was craving a hot bath. The young journalist had a thirst for adventure. Living in the city, he yearned for the quiet of his childhood village. The award is one of the most coveted in the film industry.

L.p: *Crave* = have an intense desire for something, often food; *have a thirst for* = be eager for, often knowledge or adventure; *yearn for* = long for something lost or out of reach; *covet* = badly want something that belongs to someone else, a formal word.

L.h: B Reacting to other people's emotions

L.p: *Defuse* = reduce the tension in a difficult situation; *placate* = calm an angry person down; *conciliate* = try to bring opposing sides together, a formal word; *appease* = give in to demands in order to keep the peace, often disapproving.

L.e: The manager made a joke to defuse the tension in the meeting. The airline offered free meals to placate the angry passengers. A mediator was appointed to conciliate between the two sides. Some historians argue that appeasing aggressive leaders only encourages them. The protesters remained implacable and refused to compromise.

L.tip: From *placate* comes *implacable*: impossible to change or calm: his implacable hatred for his rival. (*Placable* doesn't exist.)

L.p: *Exultant* = triumphantly happy after a success, a formal word; *ecstatic* = extremely happy and excited; *rejoice* = celebrate with great joy, a formal or literary word; *jubilant* = showing great joy, especially after winning; *bliss* = complete happiness: a week of sheer bliss. *Blissfully* often comes before *happy*, *unaware* or *ignorant*: She was blissfully unaware of the problem.

L.e: Informal: Dad has been full of the joys of spring since he retired. My grandmother was thrilled to bits with her birthday card. After passing her driving test, Zoe was walking on air for days.

L.p: *Pregnancy* begins with *conception*, when the mother's egg is *fertilised* and an *embryo* implants in the *womb* (medical: *uterus*). Most women *conceive* naturally; some are helped by *fertility drugs* or *IVF* (in vitro fertilisation; babies born this way are sometimes called *test tube babies*). The *foetus* is fed through the *placenta*. After 40 weeks the mother *goes into labour*; if not, she may be *induced*. A *midwife* usually helps her *give birth*; sometimes a surgeon *delivers* the baby by *caesarean section*.

L.x: *Expect* meaning 'expect a baby' is only used in the continuous form: Helena *is expecting* (not *expects*) a baby in October.

L.e: My great-uncle lived to a ripe old age; he was 101 when he died. As a pensioner he moved into sheltered accommodation, but he was never doddery and had all his wits about him until the end. Sadly, his younger brother developed dementia in his eighties. After the funeral, the family held a wake in the village pub. He had asked for a cremation, not a burial.

L.p: *Late* = now dead; *sheltered accommodation* = housing for old people with care staff; *doddery* = weak and unsteady (informal); *dementia* = an illness that causes memory loss; *coffin* = the box a dead person is put in; *wake* = a gathering after a funeral; *mourning* = expressing sadness after a death (the *mourners* have been *bereaved*); *cremation* = burning the body (as opposed to *burial*).

Expressing sympathy: *My condolences* (formal) or *I'm so sorry for your loss*. A gentle way to say *die*: *pass away*. Informal and humorous: *on your last legs* (also used of old machines). In news reports: *fatalities* (deaths in an accident or disaster) and *perish* (die, especially in a disaster). In legal language: *the deceased* (the person who has died), *bequeath* (leave something to someone in a will) and *die intestate* (die without making a will).

L.p: Students often look *scruffy* (= untidy) in jeans, but in business they must learn the *dress codes* of the workplace. *Business attire* (formal = clothing) should project a professional image: avoid clothes that *reveal* too much *cleavage* or your *midriff* (= the part between the chest and the waist), and *see-through fabrics*, though nobody wants to look *frumpy* (= old-fashioned and boring). A good choice of *outfits* and suits is *invaluable* (= extremely useful), and *accessories* such as *cufflinks* complete the look. Some offices have *dress-down days*; some jobs need *protective clothing* such as *overalls* and safety helmets.

L.tip: Careful: *invaluable* does not mean 'not valuable' – it means 'extremely useful': Her advice was invaluable. Something with no value is *worthless*.

L.h: B Words and expressions about clothes

L.p: Clothes can be *revealing* (showing a lot of flesh), *skimpy* (short, using little material), *baggy* (loose), *clingy* (close-fitting) or *chic* /ʃiːk/ (modern and stylish). An invitation may ask for *smart-casual* clothes. To be *dressed up to the nines* (or *dolled up*) = dressed very fashionably or formally. Some people buy *designer label* clothes, but most buy on the *High Street* (= in ordinary shops). Clothes can be *made-to-measure* or bought *off the peg* (= ready-made).

L.e: Wide-leg trousers are all the rage this season. Her wedding dress was the height of fashion. The singer is a real trend-setter: whatever she wears, teenagers copy. Wireless earbuds were last year's must-have item. Not every new style catches on. My cousin is a slave to fashion and buys something new every week.

L.p: Clothing idioms: speaking *off the cuff* means without any preparation; if one person is *hand in glove with* another, they work very closely together, often in a secret or dishonest way; doing something *on a shoestring* means with very little money; a *no-frills* service offers only the basics; and if you *have something up your sleeve*, you are keeping a secret plan or idea ready to use later.

L.p: *Housewarming* = a party you give after moving into a new home; *stag party* = the groom's night out with male friends before a wedding; *hen night* = the bride's celebration with female friends; *girls' night out* = an evening when a group of women go out together; *fancy dress* = costumes worn for fun; *reception* = the formal party after a wedding ceremony; *black-tie* = requiring formal evening clothes; *launch party* = a celebration to introduce a new product or book; *leaving do* = an informal party for someone who is leaving a job.

L.e: We're having a housewarming party on Saturday to celebrate our new flat. My brother's stag party is in Dublin, and his fiancée's hen night is in fancy dress. The firm is throwing a launch party for its new app, and there's a leaving do for Sam on Friday.

At conferences, Leo is always networking: he exchanges business cards with everyone and regularly does lunch with clients. His colleague prefers to hobnob with senior managers, hoping to rub shoulders with the people who make decisions. Being proactive has helped them both.

L.p: *Socialising* is meeting people for pleasure; *networking* is making contacts that will be useful for your business or career. *Hobnob with* = be friendly with someone important (sometimes disapproving); *rub shoulders with* = mix socially with; *proactive* = taking action yourself rather than waiting.

L.p: *Overrated* = not as good as people say; *hackneyed* = used so often it is boring; *disjointed* = unconnected and hard to follow; *far-fetched* = impossible to believe; *risqué* /rɪˈskeɪ/ = slightly shocking; *gripping* = exciting from start to finish; *harrowing* = extremely upsetting; *moving* = making you feel sad or full of pity; *understated* = simple but attractive; *tedious* = boring; *hilarious* = extremely funny.

L.e: In my opinion, the award-winning novel is overrated. The storyline of the new detective series is hackneyed – we've seen it a hundred times. The documentary about the earthquake was harrowing. L.tip: Most of these adjectives also work for books and plays: The ending of the play was far-fetched.

L.e: When the curtain fell, the applause went on for minutes, and the cast returned for an encore. The young violinist received a standing ovation and glowing reviews. Critics say his first novel is a masterpiece, and he's described as an up-and-coming talent. The actor fears being typecast as a villain.
Her early films were lauded, but her latest was panned by the critics. The musical bombed on Broadway and closed after a week – a complete flop. Many reviewers felt that the lead actor was miscast.

L.p: People have always been suspicious of new art movements. At the end of the 19th century people were shocked by *Impressionism* and called its *practitioners* careless *daubers* (= people who paint quickly and badly). L.p: The *blurb* is the short description printed on the back of a book (or online) to persuade you to read it, often with praise from reviewers.

L.e: A poignant story about a girl caring for her grandfather. This acclaimed author's latest novel is a compelling thriller set in a remote Scottish village. A chilling, macabre tale of a house that remembers. A lugubrious chronicle of a failing farm, with a surprisingly hopeful ending. A real page-turner, full of fresh insight into family life. The narrator's wry humour makes this an engaging read. Ella, the eponymous protagonist of 'Ella's War', is an enigmatic figure.

L.p: *Poignant* = moving and sad; *chronicle* = a description of events in order; *acclaimed* = praised; *compelling* = very interesting; *lugubrious* = dark and gloomy; *macabre* = concerned with death, often cruel; *page-turner* = a book that keeps you reading; *enigmatic* = mysterious; *wry* = amused in the face of a bad situation; *eponymous* = having the same name as the title; *protagonist* = main character.

*Journal* = a record of what you do each day, or a regular academic publication; *memoirs* /ˈmemwɑːz/ = a written account of your own life, often by a politician or military leader; *encyclopedia* = articles in alphabetical order on all knowledge; *anthology* = a collection of poems or stories by different authors; *manual* = a technical book of instructions; *logbook* = a record of events, e.g. the journeys of a ship.

L.x: An academic publication issued regularly is called a *journal* (not *magazine*).

L.p: As food production becomes more industrialised, labels matter more. Words like *wholesome* (= good for you) and 'homemade' can be vague, and the numbering system for *additives* (= substances added to improve taste or appearance) is often incomprehensible. Some descriptions have a clear official meaning: *wholefoods* (with nothing taken away or added), *free-range* eggs (from hens that can move around outside), *gluten-free* bread, 'no artificial *preservatives*' (= chemicals that stop food decaying).

Clear labelling matters to many shoppers: people with food allergies (who are *allergic to* nuts, for example), *vegans*, who avoid all animal products, buyers who want *unprocessed* food, and anyone worried about *animal welfare* who refuses eggs from *battery farming* (hens kept in tiny cages). As *convenience food* grows more popular, colour-coded labels help: red means a high level of fat, sugar or salt, and green a low one. *Fair trade* goods promise farmers a fair price.

L.e: Asking my two brothers to share a car was a recipe for disaster. The children cooked up an excuse for being late. Opera isn't my cup of tea, I'm afraid. The journalists grilled the minister about the missing money. It sounds like another half-baked plan to me. A few jokes would spice up your speech. The bar was full of unsavoury types. L.p: Flying: you can travel with a national airline or a *budget airline*, on a direct *route* or *via* another city (Rome via Paris). The cheapest tickets are often *non-refundable*, and changing them means paying a *cancellation fee*. A *stopover* is a short stay in a city on the way to your destination. Holiday prices often include *transfers* between the airport and the hotel, and an *all-inclusive* deal covers all your food and drink too. When you compare deals, think about *value for money*.

L.p: Plant metaphors: the *seeds of* something are its beginnings (the seeds of a revolution). L.h: B A definition of one belief: pacifism

L.h: A Specialist terms for talking about language

L.p: *Syntax* = grammar and word order; *phonology* = the sound system; *lexicon* = vocabulary; *orthography* = writing systems and spelling; *morphology* = how words are formed.

L.e: Linguists study syntax (how words combine into sentences) and phonology (the sound system of a language). The sounds /p/ and /b/ are different phonemes in English because they change meaning: pat, bat. The vowel in 'boy' is a diphthong, a sound that glides from one vowel to another. Japanese writing mixes several systems, including characters borrowed from Chinese. The word 'replayed' has three morphemes: re-, play and -ed.

L.h: B Describing how words are used

L.p: A *polysemous* word has several related meanings – think of *head* (of a body, of a company, of a queue). The *context* tells you which meaning is intended. Words can be used *literally* or metaphorically: a literal bridge crosses a river; a bridge between cultures does not. Language *usage* keeps changing: some words become *obsolete*, and new ones are *coined* all the time. *Register* is the level of formality, and *jargon* is the specialist vocabulary of a profession, such as legal or medical jargon.

L.h: C Using language well or badly

L.p: *Articulate* = good at expressing thoughts in clear words; *eloquent* = speaking or writing in a powerful and moving way; *succinct* = brief but clear; *inarticulate* = unable to express yourself clearly; *lost for words* = so surprised or moved that you cannot speak. *The mot juste* (from French) is the perfect word for a situation, and if you *put your foot in it*, you say something tactless that causes embarrassment.

L.h: A History: the great and the ordinary

L.p: *Archaeologists* dig up and study objects left by people in the past. Their finds help us understand ancient *empires* (huge areas ruled by one power) and *dynasties* (series of rulers from one family). Since *the dawn of civilisation*, people have recorded the *reign* of each ruler, the *heir* who would take over, the *coronation* of a new king or queen, and military *conquests*. Many of these records survive as *manuscripts* (documents written by hand). Ordinary farm workers, or *peasants*, are often missing from these records; sometimes there is not a *shred of evidence* about their lives.

The lives of ordinary people – *peasants* (who worked on the land), *labourers*, the *migrations* of social groups – often go unrecorded, and historians must interpret whatever *shreds* (= very small amounts) of evidence remain.

L.e: Tools from the Bronze Age were found near the river. The castle is a fine example of medieval architecture. Florence is famous for its Renaissance palaces and paintings. The museum shows art from the pre-colonial period.

L.p: *Infantry* = soldiers on foot; *cavalry* = soldiers on horses (both uncountable); *armour* = metal protective clothing; *chariot* = a two-wheeled vehicle pulled by horses; *galleon* = a large sailing ship of the 15th–18th centuries.

*Warlord* = a military commander who controls a region by force; *merchant* = a trader who bought and sold goods in large quantities, often abroad; *monarch* = a king, queen or emperor; *the nobility* = the class of people with titles such as duke or countess.

L.p: The United Nations says that 'fundamentally, poverty is a denial of choices and opportunities, a violation of human dignity'. *Absolute poverty* means being poor by a fixed minimum standard, the *poverty line*; *relative poverty* means being poor compared with people around you; *extreme poverty* (also *penury*) means living below the poverty line; *human poverty* includes *shelter*, *nutrition*, *literacy*, *sanitation*, and access to education and healthcare.

In the poorest areas, many children are *malnourished* because their diet lacks basic nutrients, and families may lack clean water, decent *shelter* and proper *sanitation* (toilets and drains). Communities without these basics are described as *deprived*.

L.h: B Other expressions relating to wealth and poverty

L.e: While the super-rich buy islands, millions of people live on the breadline. My grandparents remember a time when the whole village was poverty-stricken. The charity runs schools in impoverished mountain regions. After the war, thousands were left destitute. As students we lived from hand to mouth. Since my hours were cut, money has been tight, so we're tightening our belts. Those in the top income bracket pay the highest tax rate. The town's new affluence is visible in its expensive cars.

L.x: To talk about groups of people, use *the* + adjective with no *-s*: The tax will hit *the poor* (not *the poors*) hardest.

L.p: In a democracy, citizens can *have their say* in many ways. They can *lobby* (try to persuade) members of parliament, including *peers* in an upper chamber; sign a *petition* asking for change; and comment on proposed *legislation*. A *bill* (a draft law) passes through several stages, including a *committee stage*, where a small group of members *scrutinise* (examine in detail) every clause.

Lobbying ranges from sending letters and providing *briefing material* to organising *rallies* (= large political meetings or demonstrations). In the end, the decision is *down to* (= the responsibility of) the MP's own judgement and the influence of party policy.

L.e: Before the debate, each member received briefing material from researchers. Thousands of supporters held a rally outside parliament. In the end, the result came down to a handful of votes. Our MP holds regular meetings with her constituents. Members argued for hours in the debating chamber, but there was little substantive discussion of the costs.

L.p: Parliamentary committees examine government *policy* and spending. Some cross *departmental boundaries*, for example by carrying out an environmental *audit* of every department. Others investigate *allegations* (claims not yet proved) about the *conduct* (behaviour) of members. Committees often draw on the *expertise* of members with specialist knowledge. In some systems, opposition politicians *shadow* government ministers, following their work closely. A country's *constitution* sets out its basic laws and principles.

L.p: International organisations are often *constituted* (formally created) after a crisis. From their *foundation*, they may *pursue* aims such as keeping peace, *establishing* good relations between nations and improving life for *humanity* as a whole.

They usually prefer *negotiation* to force, oppose *injustice* and *uphold* (defend) the rights of *minorities*. Military *intervention* is normally a last option, used only when other methods have failed.

A *political movement* brings together people who share a cause. Movements often adopt a short, memorable *slogan*. Their goal may be the *liberation* of an oppressed group or the inclusion of people who feel *excluded*. Supporters show *solidarity* by marching, striking or signing petitions together.

L.e: Delegates from forty countries met in Geneva to discuss how to protect the infrastructure of coastal cities from rising seas. Governments have undertaken to share their research. The question of who pays is undeniably delicate, and, as is customary, the final statement was agreed only on the last night.

L.p: War is often a *last resort* when *diplomacy* and *economic sanctions* have failed. Even the best-planned operations with hi-tech *weaponry* cause *civilian casualties*. *Military intervention* may aim at *regime change*, but leaders of *tyrannical* regimes are often the hardest to *overthrow*.

*Civil war* often begins with *civil unrest* and *clashes* between *rival* ethnic or religious groups, and may *escalate* (= become more serious) into *all-out* war, ending in *brutal suppression* or even *ethnic cleansing* and *massacres*. *Conflict resolution* may take years, and *mistrust* and hatred may continue long after.

L.e: The two kingdoms waged war on each other for decades. Hostilities ended only after years of bloodshed. The army besieged the city for six months. Rebels ambushed a supply convoy in the mountains. Both sides agreed to a truce over the holiday, and later a ceasefire was signed. An international peacekeeping force now patrols the border.
The council is waging war on litter. Fans besieged the hotel where the band was staying. The two phone giants are battling for market supremacy.

L.p: *Sustainable development* aims to improve people's lives without damaging the environment for future generations. In many developing regions, strong *economic growth* and rising *foreign direct investment* (money that companies from abroad put into local businesses) have created jobs, yet millions still live in *abject poverty*. Governments and aid agencies *tackle* the problem in different ways: some *allocate funds* to schools and clinics, others offer *development grants* to countries that *pursue a policy* of fighting corruption.

When a country borrows more than it can repay, the *debt burden* becomes crushing. A government that *incurs* new *debt* every year may never escape. *Debt relief* – cancelling or reducing what is owed – can give a *debtor nation* the chance to invest in its own future.

A *free trade agreement* removes taxes on goods traded between countries. Disputes start when one side accuses the other of *restrictive practices*, such as secret limits on imports. If talks fail, a *trade war* can follow, with tariffs or even an *embargo* (a complete ban on trade in certain goods), which may not be *lifted* for years. Some neighbouring countries form a *monetary union* and share a single currency.

A *war-torn* economy has been badly affected by war; an *ailing* economy is in a bad state. *Devaluation* of the currency (= reducing its value against others) may be necessary. Economies may go into *recession* and not *emerge from* it for years, or suffer a *double-dip* recession (one that ends and begins again). A *slump in prices* may hurt exports, and lower taxes may *boost the economy*.

L.x: The verb is *devalue the currency* (not *devaluate the currency*).

units.sub: strapped for cash, bounced, golden handshake

L.e: I'm always broke by the end of the month. My cousin won the lottery – she's rolling in it now! When I was a student, I was always strapped for cash. My rent payment bounced because there wasn't enough in my account. Please make the cheque payable to 'City Theatre'. You can also pay by electronic transfer. Shall I charge the hotel room to my card?

L.p: *Broke* (informal) and *skint* (very informal) = with no money; *rolling in it* = having a lot of money; *strapped for cash* = with very little money; a cheque *bounces* when the bank refuses to pay it; *APR* = annual percentage rate of interest; a card *expires* on its *expiry date*; a *debit card* takes money directly from your account; a *store card* is a credit card for one shop.

L.e: Check the expiry date on your debit card before you travel. I withdrew £100 from a cashpoint at the station. The store card has a very high APR, so pay it off quickly. Most shops now accept contactless payments. If you notice unusual payments, report them as possible credit card fraud.

L.h: A Sections in newspapers and magazines

L.p: Parts of a newspaper: an *obituary* is an article about the life of someone who has recently died; the *editorial* expresses the paper's own opinion; *coverage* is the amount of attention a paper gives to an event; *classified ads* are short private advertisements grouped by type (jobs, cars, flats); a *supplement* is an extra magazine or section; a *feature* is a longer article on a particular subject; readers write to an *agony aunt* about personal problems; and *circulation* is the number of copies a paper sells.

L.e: The paper published a long obituary of the novelist. Today's editorial criticises the government's housing policy. The election got wall-to-wall coverage on TV. L.p: There are several types of journalism: *print journalism* (newspapers and magazines), *broadcast journalism* (radio and TV), *online journalism*, and *citizen journalism*, where ordinary people use social media to report and share news. Journalists get stories from *pressure groups* that want to *air their views*, and at *press conferences*, where people *issue a statement* or a *press release*. People *seeking publicity* try to include a *soundbite* (= a short, memorable phrase).

Journalists *hunt for* stories by *tapping sources* and *monitoring* news agencies. An important story gets more *airtime* and more *column inches*: more *coverage*. *Paparazzi* follow celebrities to photograph them.

Informal and critical words for newspapers: a *rag* is a low-quality paper, and *the gutter press* means papers that focus on scandal and celebrity gossip. Reporters write *copy* (the text of articles) to a deadline before the paper *goes to press* (is printed). A *back copy* is an earlier issue. A *scoop* is an important story that one paper publishes before all the others. A story *breaks* when it first becomes public, and big stories *hit the headlines*. Publishing false statements that damage someone's reputation is *libel*. *Spin* is presenting information in a way that favours one side, and *muck-raking* means searching for scandal.

L.tip: *Media* was originally plural (The media are…), but singular use is now common, especially with *social media*: Social media is changing politics. It also works before other nouns: media attention, media coverage.

L.p: *Primary care* is the first level of healthcare: the family doctor (or *physician*) and the nurses you see at a local surgery, or who make a *home visit* if you're too ill to travel. When your usual doctor is away, a *locum* (a temporary doctor) takes their place. Doctors deal with *acute* illnesses, which start suddenly and are severe, and *chronic* ones, which last a long time. For specialist treatment, your doctor will *refer* you to a hospital consultant.

*Alternative* or *complementary medicine* differs from conventional Western medicine: *acupuncturists* use needles; *chiropractors* press joints, especially the spine; *homeopathic* doctors use tiny amounts of natural substances; *aromatherapists* use oils and massage.

In the UK, most healthcare is funded by taxes and *national insurance* contributions. Seeing your *GP* (general practitioner) at the *surgery* is free, though adults in England usually pay a fixed *prescription charge* for medicines. People who can afford it sometimes *go private* to be seen more quickly.

L.p: *Hurt* describes pain, especially from an injury: My knee hurts where I fell. *Ache* is a dull pain that goes on for a while: My legs ache after the hike. L.e: Read this leaflet before you start the tablets. Tell your pharmacist if you have asthma, any heart or kidney disorder, or a medical history of stomach problems. The tablets are low-dose, but do not exceed the stated dose. Possible side effects include headaches and mild nausea. If you notice an allergic reaction, such as a rash or swelling, or any feeling of disorientation, stop the treatment and contact a doctor at once. Elderly patients have a greater risk of adverse reactions.

L.p: *Low-dose* = containing a small amount of the drug; *asthma* = a condition that narrows the airways; *medical history* = the record of your past illnesses and treatment; *disorder* = a condition that stops the body or mind working normally; *adverse reaction* = a harmful response to a medicine; *exceed* = go beyond a limit; *side effect* = an extra effect of a medicine that you did not want; *disorientation* = confusion about where you are or what is happening.

Social problems are often described as illnesses. The rise in car thefts is a *symptom* of a deeper problem; his behaviour is *symptomatic* of a lack of confidence. Problems can be *diagnosed*, and the likely outlook is the *prognosis*. An *ailing* organisation has a lot of problems. A *rash* of burglaries = many at the same time. World Cup *fever* = great excitement; preparations *reached fever pitch*.

L.e: After years of broken promises, voters have a jaundiced view of politicians. The constant arguments left the children emotionally scarred. Her laughter infected the whole room. A good editor keeps her finger on the pulse of what readers want. The strike is symptomatic of deeper problems in the industry.

L.p: *Arteries* are the *blood vessels* that carry blood away from the heart. Fatty deposits can *clog* them (block them) and *impede* (slow down) the flow of blood, raising the risk of heart attacks. High levels of *cholesterol* in the blood make this more likely. Foods such as cheese and red meat are *nutritious* but high in fat, so they are best eaten *in moderation*. Foods rich in *fibre*, such as beans, oats and whole grains, can help *counteract* the harmful effects.

Regular *cardiovascular* exercise, such as swimming or cycling, strengthens the heart and lungs. It can help people who are *diabetic* control their blood sugar, and it *burns calories*. You don't need to be *sporty*: a *brisk* walk every day makes a difference. Exercise also speeds up your *metabolism*, the process by which your body turns food into energy. If you're *intent on* (determined about) getting fit, build up slowly.

L.p: In a *smart home*, lights, heating and locks can be controlled from a phone or set to work automatically. *Interplanetary* travel means journeys between planets, and *space tourism* lets wealthy travellers pay for trips into space. *Nanotechnology* builds materials and devices at the scale of atoms and molecules, for example tiny sensors that travel through the bloodstream.

L.p: Verbs of fast movement: to *dash* or *tear* somewhere is to go there in a great hurry; to *nip* somewhere is to go there briefly (I'll nip to the shop); to *dart* is to move suddenly and quickly, like a fish or a bird; vehicles *whizz* past; a frightened person or animal *bolts* (runs away suddenly); a vehicle out of control *careers* down a hill; small animals *scurry* with short, quick steps. To *accelerate* is to go faster, and it can describe growth or change too.

L.e: I overslept and dashed to the bus stop. She tore down the stairs when she heard the news. Can you nip out and buy some milk? A lizard darted under a rock. Motorbikes whizzed along the seafront. The horse bolted when a car horn sounded. A runaway lorry careered across the road. Crabs scurried across the sand. Inflation has accelerated this year.

L.h: B Going up or down fast

L.p: *Plunge* and *plummet* = move down fast, mostly used metaphorically: Our hopes plummeted. L.e: House prices have been creeping up for months. On the motorway, traffic crawled along at walking pace. The toddler tottered across the room. A man sidled up to me and offered to sell me a watch. Stop dawdling or we'll miss the film.

L.p: *Totter* = walk slowly and unsteadily; *sidle* = walk nervously, as if trying not to be noticed; *dawdle* = move more slowly than necessary.

units.sub: I should be so lucky, bound to, aspirations

L.h: A Expressions based on modal verbs

L.e: I must admit I was wrong about the restaurant – it's excellent. You want me to drive you to the airport at 4 a.m.? You must be joking! And who, may I ask, left the door open? Don't worry about the broken glass – accidents will happen. Win the lottery? I should be so lucky!

L.x: Remember the apostrophe: The window *won't* (not *wont*) open.

L.p: *The odds are* = it is likely that; *the odds are against* = it is unlikely; *bound to* = almost certain to; *unquestionably* = without any doubt; *apparent* = obvious; *for sure* = certainly (at the end); *in all probability* = very likely; *the chances are* = it is probable; *every likelihood* = a strong probability.

L.e: The odds are that it will rain at the weekend. With all that training, she's bound to win. He is unquestionably the best player in the team. It soon became apparent that nobody had read the report. In all probability the meeting will be postponed. The chances are the shops will be busy. There's every likelihood of delays.

L.e: It's essential to book early in summer. A visa is obligatory for all visitors. When the bridge closed, we had no option but to take the long route. Employers have an obligation to protect their staff.

L.h: A Collocations with compliment and praise

L.e: My teacher paid me a compliment on my pronunciation. When she said her cake was 'probably awful', she was fishing for compliments. 'You're very brave to wear that colour' sounds like a back-handed compliment to me. Being called 'surprisingly good' is a double-edged compliment.

L.p: Politicians who *promise the earth* (or the moon) make huge promises they can't keep. *Promise* can also mean 'show signs of': The concert promises to be a great night. A *promising* student shows signs of future success. To *anticipate* is to expect something before it happens. Witnesses in court speak *under oath*, having formally promised to tell the truth. A *pledge* is a public promise, often of money or support; a *vow* is a solemn promise, such as a wedding vow. People make *resolutions* on 1 January to *turn over a new leaf* and improve their lives. If you *go back on your word*, you fail to do what you promised.

L.e: I could have sworn I locked the door, but it was open when I got back. My grandad swears by a cold shower every morning. The film has a lot of swear words, so it isn't suitable for children. The company has pledged to plant a million trees. She vowed never to speak to him again.

L.tip: *Swear* can mean make a solemn promise or use taboo language.

L.p: To *bet* is to risk money on an unknown result; risking money on games is *gambling*. The money you risk is your *stake*; if something is *at stake*, it is at risk. A *wager* is a more formal bet. *The odds* are the chances of something happening.

L.e: If you want a quiet beach, your best bet is to go early. Will the trains run on time tomorrow? Don't bet on it! My uncle likes to have a flutter on the horses. Fancy a coffee? – You bet! Apply to several universities to hedge your bets. With his whole career at stake, he couldn't afford to fail. Gambling can become an addiction.

L.e: Since I moved abroad, I've been out of touch with most of my old classmates. I often wonder what became of my first football coach – Mr Hale, if I recall. When I think back to those Saturday mornings, I realise how patient he was. I lost touch with my best friend after university. We used to pass notes right under the teacher's nose. Old photos always take me back to our family holidays in Wales. I have only a vague memory of my grandparents' farm, but when I smell hay, it all comes back to me. What stands out in my mind is the sound of the sea at night. My parents love reminiscing about their student days, though they probably see them through rose-tinted spectacles. Hearing that song filled me with nostalgia.

L.p: *Out of touch* = not knowing what has happened recently; *what became of* = what happened to; *takes me back to* = makes me remember; *stands out in my mind* = what I remember most; *reminisce about* = talk or think about pleasant past events; *rose-tinted spectacles* = seeing only the good things; *nostalgia* = pleasure mixed with sadness when you think about the past.

L.x: Don't confuse remind and remember: The class photo *reminded me of* (not *remembered me*) my schooldays.

L.e: I regret not learning the piano when I had the chance. He felt a pang of jealousy when he saw his old girlfriend with someone else. Years later, she still rued the day she sold the house. The poem laments the loss of the old village. The whole town mourned the young firefighter.

L.h: A Presenting arguments and commenting on others' work

L.p: To *advocate* a policy is to argue publicly for it. To *deduce* is to reach a logical conclusion from the facts you have; to *infer* is to work something out from indirect evidence. Two studies that *complement* each other fit well together and fill each other's gaps, while studies that *overlap with* each other cover some of the same ground.

Describing research: *empirical* studies rely on observation and experiment rather than theory; an *ambiguous* result can be understood in more than one way; a *coherent* argument is logical and well organised; a *comprehensive* review includes everything relevant; an *authoritative* book is reliable because it is written by experts.

L.h: B Talking about figures and processes

L.p: Talking about data: an *arbitrary* choice is made randomly, without good reason; misleading graphs can *distort* the truth; the *incidence* of a disease is the rate at which it occurs; the *predominant* view is the most common one; steps that happen *in sequence* follow a set order; a *widespread* problem affects many places or people.

units.sub: reiterate, subsume, beyond the scope of

L.e: The minister reiterated that the hospital would not close. The report summarises the main findings in two pages. For many critics, the building epitomises the worst of 1970s design. L.p: *Reiterate* = repeat; *summarise* = describe the main points briefly; *epitomise* = be a perfect example of; *assert* = say firmly that something is true; *expound* = explain and develop (an idea); *underscore* = emphasise; *posit* = suggest as a basic fact; *account for* = explain.

L.e: Students from abroad comprise a third of the class. The exam consists of three papers. Several smaller topics can be subsumed under the heading 'health'. The museum's collection embraces art from five continents. Her music is hard to categorise – it's part jazz, part folk.

L.e: My mum can touch-type at seventy words a minute. The author sent the typescript to her editor. Could you run off thirty copies of the agenda? Format the headings in bold. I cut and pasted the quotes into my essay. Your username must be at least six characters long.

L.e: My sister has a thing about spiders – she won't go near one. It's only a scratch – don't make a big thing of it. The thing is, I've already promised to work this weekend. I can't come. For one thing, I'm broke; for another, I'm exhausted. Once he gets it together, he'll be a great musician. Don't worry about the tickets – I'll get it sorted.

L.h: B When you can't think of the word

L.p: When a name escapes you, informal fillers can help. For things: *thingy*, *whatsit*, *whatchamacallit*. For people: *whatsisname* (a man) or *whatsername* (a woman), and *thingy* for anyone. They're fine with friends, but not in formal situations.

L.e: Pass me the whatsit – you know, the thing for opening bottles. I met whatsername from the gym, the woman with the red bike.

L.p: Informal ways to say *a lot of*: *bags of* (time, room), *masses of*, *loads of*. *Umpteen* means a great many: umpteen emails. *A scrap of* means even a tiny amount, usually after a negative: not a scrap of evidence.

L.e: Relax – there's bags of room in the car. We had masses of food left after the party. I've told him umpteen times to lock the door. There isn't a scrap of evidence against her.

L.h: A Vague expressions for numbers and quantities

L.e: The painting sold for a sum in excess of £2 million. A new kitchen will cost somewhere in the region of £8,000. The drive takes three hours, give or take. Approximately half the members voted. We'll be away for a fortnight or so. Quite a few people turned up late. The audience was mostly young, with a smattering of older fans. Add just a smidgen of salt. She put a dollop of cream on her pie. My grandad has stacks of old records in the attic.

L.p: *In excess of* = more than (formal); *somewhere in the region of* = about; *give or take* = plus or minus (informal); *or so* = or a bit more; *quite a few* = a surprisingly large number; *a smattering of* = a small proportion of; *a dash* or *a smidgen* = a very small amount; *a dollop* = a lump of soft food; *stacks of* = a large number of (informal).

L.h: B Making things less precise in informal conversation

L.e: The kitchen is more or less finished. It was a bit of a shock to see the bill. Bring snacks, drinks or whatever. We need pens, paper, things like that. I'd like a small car – a Fiat or something along those lines. She said the plan was nonsense, or words to that effect. The shop sells candles, soaps and suchlike.

L.x: We don't usually use *more or less* with ages: He's *about 35* (not *more or less 35*).

L.tip: Other vague language: a sort of reddish colour; forty-fourish; a bit on the big side; a kind of elasticky thing; walks and that; treatments and suchlike.

L.h: A Verbs of volume: from quiet to loud

L.p: *Mumble* and *mutter* are usually negative: Stop mumbling! He was muttering under his breath. *Murmur* can be positive: They murmured their approval. *Without a murmur* = without any protest. *Raise your voice* = speak louder, or speak angrily: Don't you raise your voice at me!

To be heard, people *raise their voice*, *yell* (shout loudly, often in anger or excitement), *shriek* (make a sudden high, sharp cry) or *roar* (shout in a deep, loud voice, like a crowd at a match). When the noise is aimed angrily at someone, use *at*: The coach yelled at the players.

L.h: B Verbs for speech and styles of conversation

L.e: My mum keeps nagging me to tidy my room. The two kids bickered all the way to the beach. It's unkind to slag off your friends behind their backs. Stop whining – we'll be home soon. My grandparents chatted away for hours. The neighbours love to gossip. Don't believe him – he's just winding you up. She's buttering up the boss because she wants a day off. He tends to exaggerate. It's dangerous to generalise about a whole country.

L.p: *Nag* = keep criticising; *bicker* (or *squabble*) = argue about something unimportant; *slag off* = criticise insultingly (very informal); *whine* = complain in an annoying way; *wind someone up* = tease or fool them (a wind-up); *butter someone up* = say nice things because you want something.

L.h: A Prefixes with a clear meaning

L.p: Many English prefixes change a word's meaning in a predictable way. *In-* (and *im-* before p or m, *il-* before l, *ir-* before r) means 'not': *incapable*, *imperfect*, *illogical*, *irrelevant*. *Mis-* means 'badly' or 'wrongly': *misbehave*, *misuse*. *Out-* means 'more than': *outnumber*, *outweigh*. *Re-* means 'again': *rethink*, *redevelop*. *E-* means 'electronic': *e-commerce*, *e-reader*. *Eco-* means 'connected with the environment': *eco-friendly*, *eco-warrior*.

L.e: Wearing shorts to the funeral was completely inappropriate. The report contained several inaccuracies, and the minister's inability to explain them caused anger. In the new town, cars outnumber bicycles three to one, but the council says the benefits of the bypass outweigh the costs. The old docks will be redeveloped as flats and offices, so many shops are rethinking their plans. My aunt was a teacher who misused her authority; her pupils often misbehaved to annoy her.

L.x: The service is *irregular* (not *unregular*), and the timetable is *illogical* (not *unlogical*).

L.p: *Over-* and *under-* have three main uses. They can mean 'too much' or 'too little': *overpriced*, *overrated*, *underestimate*, *understaffed*. They can describe position: a rock that *overhangs* the path sticks out above it; something *underfoot* is under your feet. And they appear in more figurative words: if you *overstep the mark*, you go too far; an *underhand* method is secret and dishonest; to *undermine* something is to weaken it slowly. *Up-* often suggests improvement: an *upgrade*, an *upturn* in the economy.

L.e: Tickets for the festival were overpriced, and many people thought the main band was overrated. The clinic is so understaffed that patients wait for hours. Snow made the ground slippery underfoot. Her brother's success always overshadowed her own. Rumours undermined the manager's authority, and some staff accused him of underhand tactics. The economy has seen a modest upturn, so the airline is upgrading its fleet. The singer became famous almost overnight.

L.tip: *Over-* and *under-* often form pairs of opposites: overpaid / underpaid, overestimate / underestimate, overdressed / underdressed.

L.p: Some prefixes come from Latin and are less obvious. *Con-* or *com-* often means 'together' or 'with': to *converse* is to talk together, to *commiserate* is to share someone's sadness, and *condolences* are words of sympathy. *Pro-* often means 'forward': to *promote* something is to push it forward, and things that *proliferate* multiply quickly; if you *procrastinate*, you keep pushing a task forward to a later time. *E-* (or *ex-*) means 'out': to *eject* is to throw out, to *emit* is to send out.

L.e: We sent the family our condolences and commiserated with them at the funeral. Leftover gravy congeals in the fridge. A chemical leak contaminated the water supply. Food apps have proliferated in recent years. I always procrastinate when I have to write reports. The machine ejected my card and emitted a loud beep.

L.p: Some suffixes combine very freely with other words. *-able* means 'can be': *washable*, *predictable*, *avoidable*, *manageable*; *disposable* things are thrown away after use. *-conscious* means 'aware of, concerned about': *health-conscious*, *safety-conscious*, *time-conscious*, *class-conscious*. *-free* means 'without': *stress-free*, *tax-free*, *additive-free*. *-rich* means 'containing a lot of': *fibre-rich*, *calcium-rich*. *-led* means 'organised or run by': *community-led*, *student-led*. *-minded* describes attitudes and interests: *like-minded*, *career-minded*, *money-minded*, *high-minded*. *-proof* means 'protected against': *waterproof*, *soundproof*, *ovenproof*; something *idiotproof* (informal) is impossible to use wrongly. *-related* means 'connected with': *age-related*, *stress-related*. *-ridden* means 'full of' something bad: *crime-ridden*, *guilt-ridden*, *bedridden*. *-worthy* means 'deserving': *newsworthy*, *praiseworthy*.

L.e: Most of these injuries are avoidable if workers wear the right equipment. Health-conscious customers look for additive-free, fibre-rich products. The festival was a student-led event, and it was surprisingly stress-free. I joined an online group of like-minded gardeners. The new coffee machine is idiotproof – even I can use it. Since the factory closed, the area has become crime-ridden. After the accident he felt guilt-ridden for months. The rescue was hardly newsworthy, but the firefighters' courage was praiseworthy.

L.x: Use a singular noun in the first part: *a student-led protest* (not *a students-led protest*).

L.h: B Suffixes that make adjectives, people nouns and verbs

L.p: *-ly* can form adjectives as well as adverbs: *lively*, *costly*, *leisurely*, *miserly*. *-ant* (and *-ent*) can describe a person who does something: an *applicant* applies for something, a *claimant* claims money, an *informant* gives information, a *contestant* takes part in a competition, an *occupant* lives in or uses a place. *-en* turns adjectives into verbs (*moisten*, *sweeten*, *worsen*, *redden*) and nouns into adjectives describing materials (*woollen*, *golden*, *wooden*).

L.e: We had a leisurely walk along the canal. The repairs turned out to be costly. Every applicant must send two references. One contestant answered all the questions correctly. The police relied on an informant inside the gang. The previous occupants left the flat in perfect condition. Moisten the edges of the pastry with water. The patient's condition worsened during the night. She wore a red woollen hat.

L.tip: Words with *-ly* like *lively* and *costly* are adjectives, so they have no adverb form: say *in a friendly way* (not *friendlily*).

L.p: Many words, especially in science and academic English, are built from parts that come from Greek or Latin. Unlike the suffixes in Unit 87, you cannot use most of these freely to make new words, but recognising them helps you guess meanings.

L.e: The island is an autonomous region with its own parliament. Supermarkets now offer biodegradable bags. Cybercrime costs businesses billions every year. Low pay and long hours demotivate staff. Her monograph on medieval bridges took six years to write. My grandfather's technophobia means he refuses to use a smartphone. The tax change is retroactive, so it applies from last April.

L.tip: Knowing word parts helps with long words: *bio-* + *-logy* = biology; *tele-* + *-phon-* = telephone; *auto-* + *-graph* = autograph (writing by yourself, i.e. a signature).

L.p: A *blend* joins parts of two words into a new one. *Brunch* (breakfast + lunch) is a late morning meal; a *heliport* (helicopter + airport) is a landing place for helicopters; *smog* (smoke + fog) is polluted air over a city; a *motel* (motor + hotel) is a roadside hotel for drivers; a *webinar* (web + seminar) is an online seminar; a *guesstimate* (guess + estimate) is a rough estimate; a *docudrama* (documentary + drama) is a drama based on real events; a *breathalyser* (breath + analyser) measures alcohol on a driver's breath.

L.e: On Sundays we meet friends for brunch. The hospital roof has a heliport for air ambulances. On still winter days, smog hangs over the city. We stayed at a cheap motel off the motorway. Three hundred people joined the webinar. My guesstimate is that the job will take a month. The docudrama follows the rescue of the trapped miners. The driver refused to take a breathalyser test.

L.h: A Where English words come from

L.p: A language's *lexicon* is its whole stock of words. English has an unusually mixed *word stock*: its core is Old English, but invaders, traders and scholars have *enriched* it over many centuries with words from dozens of *sources*. Norse and Norman French *had a* huge *impact on* everyday vocabulary, and later scholars added many words *of classical origin* (from Latin and Greek). A word that one language adopts from another is a *loanword*, also known as a *borrowing*. One *linguistic* result is that English often has several words for one *concept*: *ask* (Old English), *question* (French), *interrogate* (Latin).

L.e: The exhibition traces the sources of everyday English words. Trade with Asia enriched the language with words for spices and fabrics. Social media keeps adding new terms to the lexicon, and television had a lasting impact on the way people speak. 'Democracy' is a word of classical origin, while 'sky' is a borrowing from Old Norse.

L.p: English has borrowed words from almost every language its speakers have met: *amber* (from Arabic), *roster* (Dutch), *shampoo* (Hindi), *karaoke* and *tycoon* (Japanese), *palaver* (Portuguese, = unnecessary fuss), *hammock* (Spanish, from a Caribbean language), *yoghurt* (Turkish), *safari* (Swahili) and *robot* (Czech).

L.e: Check the staff roster to see who's working on Saturday. We spent the afternoon in a hammock under the palm trees. Getting a visa was such a palaver – three forms and two interviews! The bar has a karaoke night every Friday. She wore a necklace of polished amber. The shipping tycoon owned three islands.

L.p: *False friends* are words that look alike in two languages but mean different things. English *sensible* means 'practical and reasonable' (French *sensible* means 'sensitive'); a *library* lends books rather than selling them (compare Spanish *librería*, a bookshop); *eventually* means 'in the end', not 'possibly'; and *embarrassed* means 'uncomfortable and self-conscious', while Spanish *embarazada* means pregnant.

L.x: If you mean 'perhaps', say *I might come* (not *I will eventually come*) to the party.

L.p: English is now a *global language* and a *lingua franca*: a shared language for people with different *mother tongues*, for example at international conferences or in multinational companies. It exists in many *varieties* – British, American, Indian, Nigerian, Singaporean and more – sometimes called *World Englishes*. In fact, *non-native speakers* of English now far outnumber native speakers.

L.e: At the summit, English was the lingua franca for delegates from thirty countries. Singapore English is a lively variety with its own words and expressions. Her mother tongue is Tagalog, but she writes novels in English.

L.h: A Pairs that look and feel alike

L.p: Some pairs of words are similar in form and meaning, so learners mix them up. To *intervene* is to get involved in order to help or stop something, and it is fairly neutral; to *interfere* is to get involved where you are not wanted, and it is critical. *Continually* means happening again and again, often annoyingly; *continuously* means without any break. A *series* is a set of programmes on one subject, each complete in itself; in a *serial*, one story continues from episode to episode. *Shade* is a cool area protected from the sun; a *shadow* is the dark shape made when something blocks light, and *in the shadow of* can suggest being dominated by something. To *compliment* someone is to praise them; to *complement* something is to go well with it and make it better.

L.e: The referee had to intervene when the players started pushing. My neighbour is always interfering in other people's business. The printer has been breaking down continually all week. The machine runs continuously, twenty-four hours a day. There's a new nature series on TV about the oceans. I missed two episodes of the crime serial, so I've lost track of the plot. Let's sit in the shade. The village lies in the shadow of a huge power station. Everyone complimented the chef on the soup. The sauce complements the fish perfectly.

L.x: The waiter *complimented* (not *complemented*) us on our choice of wine.

L.p: *Moist* describes something pleasantly wet (a moist chocolate cake); *damp* describes things that are a little wet in a cold, unpleasant way (damp walls). The *theme* of a book, festival or event is the main idea that runs through it; a *topic* is the subject that people talk or write about. *Security* is about protection from crime and attack; *safety* is about protection from accidents and harm. You *avoid* something by staying away from it; you *evade* something, more formally, by escaping from it, often dishonestly (evade tax, evade capture).

L.e: Keep the soil moist but not soaking. The cellar smells damp. The theme of this year's carnival is 'the ocean'. Politics is not a good topic for a first date. Airport security checked every bag. For safety reasons, please keep your seat belt fastened. I always avoid the motorway on Fridays. The businessman was jailed for evading tax.

L.h: C Phrasal verbs and their nouns

L.p: Nouns formed from phrasal verbs do not always have the meaning you expect, and sometimes the parts swap places. *Break out* gives two nouns: a *breakout* (an escape, e.g. from prison) and an *outbreak* (a sudden start of something unpleasant, such as disease or war). *Look out* gives a *lookout* (a person watching for danger) and an *outlook* (the likely future, or a person's attitude). *Set up* gives a *set-up* (the way something is organised). *Turn out* gives a *turnout* (the number of people who come to an event).

L.e: There was an outbreak of flu at the school. Two prisoners were recaptured after the breakout. One thief acted as a lookout while the others broke in. The economic outlook for next year is uncertain. I don't understand the set-up in this office – who's in charge? The turnout for the election was only 40%.

L.h: A Polysemy: one form, several meanings

L.p: Many common English words have several meanings; linguists call this *polysemy*. The meanings are often related – a *sharp* knife, a *sharp* mind and a *sharp* bend all involve something cutting or sudden – but sometimes they are not, and you may need a different translation for each. Words with the same spelling but completely unrelated meanings are *homographs*.

L.e: fair: The referee's decision wasn't fair. / We went to the book fair in the city centre. / She has fair hair and burns easily. / The weather should stay fair all weekend. flat: They live in a flat above the bakery. / The countryside here is very flat. / I've got a flat tyre. / The singer was slightly flat on the high notes. plain: The instructions are written in plain English. / She wore a plain black dress. / The village lies on a wide plain. / He's a plain-speaking man. sharp: Be careful – that knife is sharp. / There's been a sharp rise in prices. / Turn sharp left at the church. / Come at nine o'clock sharp.

L.p: The *context* – the words and situation around a word – usually tells you which meaning is intended. When it doesn't, look at the whole dictionary entry, not just the first meaning: the most common meaning is listed first, but it may not be the one you need. Notice also that one meaning may be countable and another uncountable (*a capital* = a city; *capital* = money to start a business), or that meanings belong to different parts of speech (*mean* = intend; *mean* = unkind or ungenerous; *the mean* = the average).

L.e: You need a lot of capital to start a restaurant. Canberra is the capital of Australia. Please write your name in capital letters. I'm sorry – I didn't mean to be rude. Don't be so mean – share your sweets with your sister. The mean temperature in July is 24°C.

L.p: Writers and comedians enjoy polysemy. A *pun* (or *play on words*) uses two meanings of a word at once for humour, and many newspaper headlines and adverts depend on a *double meaning*: a bakery advert saying 'We knead you' plays on *knead* and *need*; a headline about a failed bank saying 'Bank loses its balance' plays on two meanings of *balance*.

L.e: The joke depends on a pun. The advert's slogan has a clever double meaning. Puns are hard to translate because the play on words only works in one language.

L.p: *Collocations* are words that naturally occur together. Native speakers say *heavy traffic*, not *thick traffic*, even though both could make sense. Learning a noun with its usual adjectives makes your English sound natural. For example, something authentic can be *the real thing* or *the genuine article*; you give a *broad summary* of a long report, or describe it *in great detail*; and *formidable* (impressive and rather frightening) goes with a small group of nouns: *a formidable opponent*, *a formidable reputation*, *a formidable task*, *a formidable challenge*.

L.e: After years of fake designer bags, this one is the genuine article. Instant coffee is fine, but I prefer the real thing. Could you give us a broad summary of the plan? The guidebook describes every church in great detail. Climbing the north face is a formidable challenge. The new coach has a formidable reputation.

L.p: Verbs also have favourite adverbs. We *feel strongly* about issues we care about, we *move swiftly on* to the next point in a meeting, we *deeply regret* our mistakes, and we say *if I remember rightly* when we are not completely sure of a fact.

L.e: Many parents feel strongly about school uniforms. Let's move swiftly on to the budget. The company deeply regrets the delay. If I remember rightly, the shop closes at six on Saturdays.

L.x: She was *bitterly disappointed* (not *strongly disappointed*) when she missed the final.

L.p: Intensifying adverbs prefer certain adjectives. *Utterly* (completely) is most often used with negative words: *utterly ridiculous*, *utterly pointless*, *utterly useless*, *utterly exhausted*, *utterly unacceptable*. *Highly* goes with words like *likely*, *unlikely*, *successful* and *recommended*; *fully* goes with *aware*, *qualified* and *booked*.

L.e: The idea of moving the airport is utterly ridiculous. After the night shift, I felt utterly exhausted. It's highly unlikely that the train will be on time. Are you fully aware of the risks?

L.p: Many verbs and their objects form fixed partnerships. In class you *raise your hand* (not *lift your hand*) to ask a question; scientists *draw a conclusion* from data; you *meet a deadline* when you finish on time; and people who take dangerous chances *run a risk*.

L.e: Raise your hand if you'd like a copy. It's too early to draw any conclusions. We worked all weekend to meet the deadline. Drivers who use their phones run a serious risk.

units.sub: keep an eye on, go hand in hand, food for thought

L.p: A *metaphor* describes something by speaking of it as if it were something else with similar qualities, without using *like* or *as*. When we say a manager is *drowning in* paperwork or that a crowd was *a sea of faces*, we are using metaphors: there is no water, but the image helps us picture the situation. Metaphors are *figurative*, not *literal*.

L.e: After the holiday I had a mountain of emails to answer. The news unleashed a flood of complaints. When I lost my job, my sister was my rock. From the stage, the audience was just a sea of faces.

L.h: B Metaphors that have become idioms

L.p: Many everyday idioms began as metaphors. If you are *on the ball*, you are alert and quick to react, like a player watching the ball. If you *keep a tight rein on* something, you control it closely, like a rider holding a horse. Parts of the body are especially common: the *heart* of a city is its centre, a river's *mouth* is where it meets the sea, and the *head* of an organisation is its leader. You can *have an eye for* something (be good at noticing it) or *keep an eye on* someone (watch them carefully). If something is *in safe hands*, a capable person is looking after it, and two things that *go hand in hand* are closely connected.

L.e: Our new assistant is really on the ball. The finance director keeps a tight rein on spending. Our hotel was right in the heart of the old town. The town grew up at the mouth of the river. My mother has an eye for antiques. Could you keep an eye on my bag for a moment? Don't worry – the project is in safe hands. Poverty and poor health often go hand in hand.

L.p: Some metaphors come in families. We often talk about ideas as if they were food: *food for thought* (something worth thinking about), a *half-baked* plan (not properly thought out), *digest* information (understand it slowly). We talk about arguments as if they were battles: *attack* a theory, *defend* a position, *win* or *lose* an argument. And we talk about time as if it were money: *spend*, *waste*, *save* or *invest* time.

L.e: The lecture gave me plenty of food for thought. I need time to digest all this information. Critics attacked every point in her argument, but she defended her position well. Don't waste time on things you can't change.

L.p: Informal idioms for success: a plan that *works like a dream* works perfectly; an event that *goes like clockwork* runs smoothly with no problems; a new system that is *up and running* has started working; when things *fall into place*, they begin to work out as hoped; and if things are *looking up*, the situation is improving.

L.e: The new booking system works like a dream. The wedding went like clockwork, despite the rain. The café should be up and running by June. After months of searching, everything finally fell into place: a job, a flat and a car. Business is looking up since the new road opened.

L.p: Some fixed reactions show frustration in conversation. *That's all we need!* is said ironically when one more problem arrives. *That's the last thing I wanted to hear* responds to news you were dreading. If one problem follows another, you might say *This is like a bad dream*. *It's a nightmare* describes any very difficult situation, and *What a pain!* is a common, mild complaint.

L.e: The car won't start. – Oh, that's all we need! / The flight's been cancelled. – That's the last thing I wanted to hear. / First the boiler, then the roof – this is like a bad dream. / Parking in the centre is a nightmare. / I've left my keys at work. What a pain!

L.p: If a question *throws* you, it confuses you so that you don't know what to say. A badly organised event is *a shambles*. Something you cannot explain is *a mystery to* you. People who *get their wires crossed* misunderstand each other, usually about arrangements. In conversation, *I'm not with you* and *You've lost me* both mean 'I don't follow what you're saying'.

L.e: The interviewer's last question completely threw me. The registration day was a total shambles. How she affords that car is a mystery to me. Somewhere we got our wires crossed: she went to the cinema and I waited at the café. Sorry, you've lost me. Could you explain that again?

L.p: Happy: *on cloud nine* and *over the moon* (both = extremely happy); passing an exam can be *a weight off your mind* (a relief). Low or stressed: *down in the dumps* (sad and depressed); *at the end of your tether* (so tired or annoyed that you can't cope any more). *Keep your chin up* encourages someone to stay positive.

L.e: Since the baby arrived, they've been on cloud nine. She was over the moon with her exam results. Finding a buyer for the house was a weight off my mind. He's been down in the dumps since his team lost. With three sick children, I'm at the end of my tether. Keep your chin up – things will get better.

units.t: Idioms for everyday situations and feelings

units.sub: come across as, come up against, rush into

L.p: Phrasal verbs are easiest to learn in context: when you meet one, note it in a full sentence rather than as a translation. Remember that one combination may have several meanings. *Come across* can mean 'find by chance' (I came across an old diary) or 'give an impression' (She comes across as shy). In formal writing, a one-word verb is often more suitable: *propose* rather than *put forward*, *investigate* rather than *look into*, *postpone* rather than *put off*, and *make a hasty decision* rather than *rush into* one.

L.e: I came across some old letters while I was clearing the attic. On the phone he comes across as quite rude, but he's lovely in person. The committee put forward three proposals. Don't rush into buying a house – take your time.

L.p: *Come* forms many phrasal verbs. A plan that *comes off* succeeds. If friends *come over*, they visit you (or travel from another country). If you ask *what came over* someone, you mean 'why did they behave so strangely?'. Something that *comes under* criticism or attack is criticised or attacked. An opportunity that *comes up* appears unexpectedly, and if you *come up against* a problem, you have to deal with it.

L.e: Our plan to surprise Mum came off perfectly. My cousins are coming over from Canada for the summer. Maya is normally so calm, but she threw her phone across the room – nobody knows what came over her. The new parking rules have come under heavy criticism. If a job comes up in the London office, I'll apply. The project came up against strong local opposition.

L.p: The particle often gives a clue to the meaning. *Up* can mean 'completely' or 'more' (use up, eat up, speed up); *down* can mean 'less' or 'stop' (slow down, cut down on, close down); *out* can mean 'to the end' or 'carefully' (sort out, carry out, work out); *on* often means 'continue' (carry on, keep on, go on); *off* often means 'leave' or 'separate' (set off, see someone off).

L.e: We've used up all the milk. The doctor told him to cut down on salt. The shop closed down last year. Researchers carried out a survey of 2,000 drivers. Carry on reading while I make some tea. We set off at dawn.

L.tip: Learn the grammar too: some phrasal verbs take an object (*carry out a survey*), some don't (*the plan came off*), and some can be separated (*sort the problem out*).
