L.p: A word's *denotation* is its basic dictionary meaning; its *connotations* are the feelings and ideas people *associate* it *with*. Some *associations* are shared by most speakers. In politics, a *dove* is someone who prefers peaceful solutions, while a *hawk* favours force – images taken from the birds. Other associations differ between cultures (black cats, the number 13, the colour white) or are purely personal: for one person the sea means holidays, for another danger.

L.e: On defence policy, the foreign minister is a dove and the defence minister is a hawk. For many British people, rain is associated with summer holidays at the seaside. The smell of the hospital had unpleasant associations for her.

L.p: Words with the same denotation can have very different connotations, so choosing the right one shows your attitude. Compare: *slim* (positive) and *skinny* (negative); *thrifty* (careful with money – positive) and *stingy* (negative); *self-assured* and *arrogant*; *inquisitive* and *nosy*; *childlike* (innocent – positive) and *childish* (immature – negative); *famous* (neutral or positive) and *notorious* (famous for something bad); *aroma* (pleasant) and *stench* (very unpleasant).

L.e: The fashion magazine called the model slim; the tabloid called her skinny. My grandmother was thrifty, not stingy – she just hated waste. The town became notorious for its traffic jams. The aroma of fresh bread drifted out of the bakery, but the bins outside gave off a terrible stench.

L.x: His behaviour at the party was *childish* (not *childlike*); he sulked when he lost a game.

L.p: Writers and advertisers exploit connotations. Calling a building firm *cowboy builders* suggests they are careless and dishonest. Estate agents describe a tiny flat as *cosy* or *compact*, and a remote house as *secluded*. Journalists choose between *freedom fighters* and *rebels*, or *protesters* and *rioters*, depending on their point of view.

L.e: We hired cowboy builders, and the roof started leaking within a month. The advert described the cottage as 'secluded' – in fact it was miles from anywhere. The same crowd was called 'protesters' in one paper and 'rioters' in another.

L.h: A Formal, neutral and informal words

L.p: *Register* is the level of formality of a text or conversation, and it reflects the relationship between the people involved. Good communicators choose words that suit the situation. Many neutral words have formal and informal partners:

t: give it your best shot, have a crack at

L.e: The hotel requests that guests wear formal attire at dinner. I'll have a crack at fixing the printer. My other half is cooking tonight. Pack your walking gear – we're going up the mountain. The company endeavours to reply to all emails within 48 hours.

L.tip: Mixing registers sounds odd: a job application should not include *kids* or *gear*, and a text to a friend saying *I shall endeavour to attend* will sound like a joke.

L.p: Some words are much more typical of writing, others of speech. Writing (especially academic or official): *subsequently* (= later), *hence* (= so), *whereas*, *in sum*, *thus*, *prior to*. Speech: *anyway*, *kind of*, *stuff*, *you know*, *like*, *pretty* (= quite).

L.e: Written: The suspect was arrested and subsequently released. Sales fell; hence the need for new products. Spoken: Anyway, I kind of liked the film. We bought pretty good stuff at the market.

L.p: In formal emails, avoid contractions and slang, use full forms (*I would be grateful if…*) and close politely. In informal messages, short sentences, contractions and everyday words sound natural. When in doubt, choose a neutral word: it is rarely wrong.

L.e: Formal: I would be grateful if you could send the documents prior to the meeting. Informal: Can you send me the stuff before Monday?

L.p: British and American English share most of their vocabulary, but road travel is full of differences. Americans *cross the street* where British people usually *cross the road*; they walk on the *sidewalk* (British *pavement*) and cross at a *crosswalk* (British *pedestrian crossing* or *zebra crossing*). A *block* is the distance between two streets in a grid, and something *kitty-corner* (informal) is diagonally opposite. Drivers *take a left* (*turn left*), stop at an *intersection* (*junction*), fill up at a *gas station* (*petrol station*), *back up* (*reverse*) out of a *parking lot* (*car park*) and join the *Interstate* (a major road linking states; compare British *motorway*). An *overpass* is a British *flyover*.

L.e: The diner is two blocks down, kitty-corner to the gas station. Take a left at the next intersection. I scraped the car while I was backing up in the parking lot. The Interstate was closed after the storm. Walk across the overpass to reach the mall.

L.p: In the countryside, an American *trail* is a British *path* or *footpath*, and a small *creek* is a *stream*. In the city, Americans go *downtown* (to the *city centre*), push a *shopping cart* (a *trolley*) round the supermarket, and take the *elevator* (*lift*) to an *apartment* (*flat*).

L.e: We hiked a mountain trail and cooled our feet in the creek. Let's get a cab downtown. Someone left a shopping cart in the middle of the street. The elevator in our apartment building is out of order.

L.tip: You will hear and read both varieties, and many American words are now common in Britain, especially among young people. Choose one variety for your own writing and use it consistently.

L.p: Many traditional English words used *man* to refer to people in general, or named jobs as if only men did them. In professional writing today, *gender-neutral* alternatives are preferred, and in job advertisements they may be legally required. Some changes were controversial at first, but most are now normal usage.

t: the person in the street, ordinary people

L.e: The chair opened the meeting at ten. A spokesperson for the hospital confirmed the news. Three firefighters were injured in the blaze. The jacket is made of a synthetic material. The company plans to double its workforce. Ask the person in the street what they think of the new tax.

L.tip: Some words with *man* have nothing to do with gender in their meaning today, e.g. *manhandle* (= handle roughly) and *manuscript*, and people rarely change them.

L.p: *Ms* /məz/ is a title for women that, like *Mr*, does not show whether the person is married; it is the usual choice in business. Some people prefer the title *Mx*. When you don't know someone's gender, or are speaking of people in general, *they* is widely used for one person: *If a student is ill, they should email the office.* In letters to unknown readers, *Dear Sir or Madam* is still used, but many writers now prefer a role: *Dear Hiring Manager*.

L.e: The letter was addressed to Ms Jane Okoro. Each applicant must bring their passport. Somebody left their umbrella in the meeting room.

L.p: Some words carry different associations when used about men and women. *Bachelor* sounds neutral or even attractive, while the old-fashioned *spinster* sounds negative. Careful writers also avoid describing the same behaviour differently by gender – for example, calling a woman *bossy* but a man in the same role *assertive*.

L.e: The novel's heroine is described as a spinster, a word few people would use today. Reviewers praised the new manager as assertive and decisive.

L.p: A story that *hits the headlines* becomes major news almost overnight. Headlines have to grab attention in very few words, especially in the *tabloids* (mass-market papers full of photos, celebrity news and short articles). Typical features: small words such as *a*, *the* and *is* are *omitted*; the present simple describes past events to make them feel immediate (STAR QUITS SHOW); headlines can be *ambiguous*, so you have to read the story to understand them; *alliteration* (words starting with the same sound) makes them memorable (BRAVE BOY BEATS BLAZE); and *emotive* words such as *horror*, *shock* and *fury* pull readers in.

L.e: PARK PLAN FURY. SHOCK AS LOCAL CLUB FOLDS. MUM'S MIRACLE ESCAPE. HOSPITAL CHIEF QUITS. The story hit the headlines when a famous actor was involved.

L.p: Headline writers prefer short, dramatic words: *slam* (criticise strongly), *row* (a noisy argument), *probe* (an investigation), *quit* (resign), *vow* (promise firmly), *axe* (cut or end), *soar* and *plunge* (rise and fall sharply), *bid* (an attempt), *clash* (fight or disagree), *blaze* (a large fire), *oust* (force someone out of a position), *hail* (praise publicly) and *woe* (trouble and sadness).

L.e: MINISTER SLAMS BANKS. ROW OVER NEW RUNWAY. POLICE PROBE INTO MISSING FUNDS. COUNCIL TO AXE BUS ROUTES. HOUSE PRICES SOAR. SHARES PLUNGE. CHAMPION'S BID FOR FIFTH TITLE. FANS CLASH AFTER DERBY. SHOP DESTROYED IN BLAZE. TEAM HAILS NEW COACH. TRAVEL WOE AS SNOW HITS.

L.tip: *Bid*, *row*, *probe* and *clash* can be nouns or verbs in headlines, which is one reason headlines can be ambiguous: in TEACHERS ROW, is it an argument, or are they in a boat?

L.p: Many headlines contain *puns* or refer to well-known sayings, film titles or songs. A story about a bakery winning an award might be headlined A BATCH MADE IN HEAVEN; a report on bad weather ruining a cricket match might read RAIN STOPS PLAY. Such headlines reward readers who notice the double meaning.

L.e: The headline was a clever pun on a famous film title. Readers loved the play on words.

L.h: A What makes bureaucratic language difficult

L.p: *Red tape* means official rules and paperwork that seem unnecessary and slow things down. Documents from governments, banks and large companies are often hard to read because they use long, formal words instead of everyday ones, passive verbs instead of active ones (*Your application has been rejected* rather than *We have rejected your application*), and set legal phrases such as *hereby* (by this document), *the undersigned* (the person who has signed below) and *the aforementioned* (mentioned earlier).

L.e: Notice to residents: Permission to demolish the shed adjoining your property is hereby refused. Any appeal must be submitted in writing to the undersigned by 30 September. Applicants who have attained the age of 65 are not eligible for the aforementioned scheme.

L.tip: Plain English campaigners encourage organisations to write *We will contact you* instead of *You will be contacted in due course*.

L.h: B Formal words and their everyday equivalents

L.e: Works will commence on 1 March. Employment with the company will terminate on 31 December. Persons residing at this address are requested to assist the inspector. In the event of fire, leave the building forthwith.

L.h: C Getting through the red tape

L.p: When dealing with officials, it helps to know a few expressions: forms must be *completed in full* (every section filled in), documents may need to be *certified* (officially confirmed as true copies), and you may be told that your case is being *processed* or is *under review*. If you are *eligible* for something, you meet the conditions to receive it.

L.e: It took four months of red tape to register the business. Please complete the form in full and enclose certified copies of your certificates. Your application is currently under review.
